monument_type: Archaeological object(s), Stūpa or Caitya, Water architecture
description_en: A stone fountain surmounted by three stūpas from approx. 14th-15th century.The village of Bigare is located 3.5 km east of Khalaṅgā (Jumla Bajār). The fountain is found in the south-eastern end of the village, on the side of the motorable path that connects Khalaṅgā to Garjyāṅgakōṭa.The fountain (001) is surmounted by three partially dismantledstūpas(002, 003 and 004). An inscribed block of cut stone is found on site. Its reading is complicated by the eroded condition of the stone. The site has recently (before May 2022, when last surveyed) been walled. Access to thestūpasis restricted by a locked metal door.The fountain has a vertical stone facing carved with plinths and projections (skt.bhadra), similar to theśikharatemple facades. Two spouts in the upper section are connected to a buried supply pipe. The spouts are shaped with the head of amakara, similar to the medieval fountains (hiti) in the Kathmandu Valley. The ancient stone spouts were ineffective in 2014. Water was then provided by a pvc pipe piercing through the fountain's stone facing, between the stone spouts. Cement was poorly applied where the stone blocks had to be broken to instal the pipe. A copper spout with amakarahead is now replacing the pvc pipe. The new spout is executed in the traditional style of the Kathmandu valley, where it was probably acquired. On both sides of the central panel are platforms. The front side of the fountain is richly adorned with carvings of bird frieses and a couple of anthropomorphs. The latter may represented Śiva and Pārvatī or the donors of the fountain.Directly above the fountain are threestūpas. A central, largerstūpa, is set in the centre (002). South and west of it are smallerstūpas(003 and 004). The plan suggests that another two smallstūpaswere originally built east and north of the central one. This quincunx plan recalls the fivestūpasthat are said to have topped the water reservoir of Patharnauli (DLK0160). This monument was built in ŚS 1276 (1354 CE) by Deva Varmā, a ministre of king Pṛthvīmalla (r. 1338-1358) (Andolfatto 2019, p. 96;Pant 2009, 301).Fountains, known asmugrāhā, are scattered throughout the Karnali basin (Nep.dhārō), particularly in the valleys of the Kalikot and Jumla districts, so that a traveller will come across one to three during his day's walk. These types of fountains are most likely from Uttarakhand, near the monolithic temple of Ek Hatia in Almiya (Chanchani 2019: 111 and Andolfatto 2019). Their construction in Uttarakhanda dates back to the 10th century. Such water architecture seems to have appeared later in west Nepal, most likely around the 12th century. The carvings on the fountain are almost identical to the ones found on temples in Kalikot (KLK0060) and estimated to date from the 14th-15th century. Furthermore, the proposed original quincux plan of thestūpasis attested in the mid-14th century. The monuments may thus be dated from the 14th-15th century. This time period corresponds to the end of the Khaśa Malla kingdom (12th-14th century) and the beginning of the Kalyāl dynasty's rule from Jumla (15th century) (Andolfatto 2019).
